caption:
Bitcoin's last two midterm Novembers 🗳️

Americans vote today, November 3. So what did bitcoin do in the month of the last two midterm elections?

November 2018: down 36.6%. That was the month of a bitter fight over a Bitcoin Cash split.
November 2022: down 16.2%. That was the month FTX, then one of the biggest exchanges, collapsed.

Both months had a big crypto crisis of their own, so it is hard to pin the drops on the vote. And two Novembers make a story, not a pattern.

What moves your view more: politics or crypto's own news?

Data: ChartRow, Bitcoin Magazine (monthly change); Cointelegraph. Past performance does not predict future results. Not financial advice.

caption:
Over 70% odds of a Fed rate hike ⚖️

Prediction markets put the odds of a US rate hike at the Fed's December 9 meeting above 70%, as of November 3.

What a hike means: borrowing gets more expensive, and cash in savings or bonds pays more.

Why crypto cares: when safe cash pays more, risky assets like crypto have to work harder to attract money. That is why markets watch the Fed so closely.

Odds are not a decision. The October jobs report on Friday and inflation data on November 10 can move them.

Save this for the next time someone says "the Fed".

caption:
Stocks rose. Bitcoin sat still 📊

Here are the big moves of the US day, Tuesday, November 3, while Americans voted.

Nasdaq: up 0.8%, as chip stocks bounced back. S&P 500: up 0.4%. Dow: down 0.4%.
Bitcoin: about flat, near $77,000 at the US close.

Under the surface, about $366M of borrowed crypto bets were force closed in 24 hours, most of them bets on prices going up. That is a liquidation: when a leveraged bet moves too far the wrong way, the exchange closes it.

A flat day can still be a painful one for traders using leverage.

caption:
60% of all crypto is bitcoin 🥧

Add up the value of every coin and about 60% of it is bitcoin. On November 3 the share stood at 59.9%.

That number has a name: bitcoin dominance. Thousands of other coins share the remaining 40%.

How to read it: when dominance rises, money is moving into bitcoin. When it falls, money is moving into other coins.

It tells you where money is going, not where prices go next.

Save this for the next time someone says "altcoin season".

One company holds over 4% of all bitcoin 🟠

Strategy, the company run by Michael Saylor, now holds 849,327 bitcoin.

It added 811 more between October 26 and November 1, paying about $65.5 million, or roughly $80,846 per coin.

Why 4%? Only 21 million bitcoin will ever exist. 849,327 is just over 4% of that cap, held by one listed company.

Big holders like this matter because their buying and selling is public. Companies have to report it, so anyone can follow along.

Follow for Bitcoin in plain English.

caption:
Stocks that never close 🕰️

On November 3, US regulators cleared perpetual futures on single US stocks. The approvals cover contracts from Coinbase, Kalshi and Bitnomial.

What a perp is: a leveraged contract that tracks a price, has no end date and trades around the clock, nights and weekends included. Crypto traders have used them for years.

The catch: with borrowed money, a small move against you can close your bet.

It is not settled. A group backed by Cboe and Citadel Securities sued in New York the same day, saying these belong under the SEC.

Would you trade a stock at 3 am on a Sunday?

caption:
Zcash is about to get 3x faster ⚡

Zcash plans a network upgrade called NU7, expected around November 5 to 6 at block 3,543,405. At that block, every node switches to the new rules at once.

The headline change: a new block every 25 seconds instead of every 75, so payments confirm about three times faster.

For comparison, bitcoin still adds a block about every 10 minutes. Faster is not automatically better. Block time is a trade off every network picks on purpose.

Save this for the next time someone says "upgrade".

Sources: Bankless (Sep 18, 2026); CryptoTicker and ZIP 259 (Oct 23, 2026). The date is an estimate from the block height. Not financial advice.

From 80% to 99% offline? 🧊

After the Binance hack, South Korea's financial regulator is weighing a tougher rule: exchanges would keep about 99% of customer coins in cold wallets, up from today's legal minimum of 80%. No decision has been made yet.

Hot wallet: online, so withdrawals are fast. Also always reachable by attackers. The Binance coins were taken from hot wallets.
Cold wallet: offline. Slower to move, much harder to steal.

Some Korean exchanges are already there. Upbit held about 99.17% cold at the end of September.

The trade off: more cold storage can mean slower withdrawals on busy days.

Where do you keep yours?

Sources: crypto.news, U.Today, Nov 3, 2026 (FSC proposal; FSS data). Not financial advice.

A bet that never ends ♾️

Since November 3, Americans can trade perpetual futures on single US stocks on regulated exchanges.

A perp is a leveraged contract on a price. No end date, no closing bell: it trades around the clock.

Leverage is the part to understand. You put up a little money and control a bigger bet. If the price moves against you far enough, the exchange closes your position and the money you put up is gone. That is a liquidation.

The rules may still change: Cboe and Citadel Securities sued the same day to stop these contracts.

Save this before you ever trade one.

caption:
It started with a job interview 🎣

On November 3, Binance published its first report on the $6.34B hack. The attackers spent months inside before they struck:

June: an engineer installed a doctored version of an AI coding tool.
September: a second engineer, approached on a real job platform, opened malware hidden in a coding "test" during a fake interview.
October 20: the attackers found a key permission on another engineer's computer.
October 29: they used it, and $6.34B left Binance's wallets.

Binance says about $2.85B has been frozen or intercepted and 98% of affected assets are replaced.

The lesson: never open a file or run code from someone you just met online.

Send this to a friend who writes code.

Source: Binance's preliminary report via PYMNTS, Bitcoin.com and TokenPost, Nov 3, 2026.

caption:
Bitcoin ETFs on Election Day: $116M out 📊

US spot bitcoin ETFs saw about $116M in net outflows on Tuesday, November 3, Election Day. BlackRock's IBIT lost about $95M and Grayscale's mini trust about $53M, while Bitwise and Fidelity took in about $29M together.

That is the third outflow day in a row, after $643M on Friday, October 30, and $399M on Monday, November 2. But the pace slowed sharply.

Why it matters: ETF flows show what money in regulated funds is doing. One day is a data point; the trend over a week tells you more.

Do you watch ETF flows, or just the price?
